monitored_text: Resources / Materials / Carburizing: Definition, Process, and Applications Carburizing: Definition, Process, and Applications Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 24 min read Published July 16, 2026 Carburizing is a thermochemical heat treatment process that introduces carbon into the surface layer of low-carbon steel, raising the surface carbon concentration to produce a hardened, wear-resistant outer case while preserving a tough and ductile core. Carburizing is defined as a heat treatment process, per AGMA 923, in which austenitized steel contacts a carbonaceous atmosphere with enough carbon potential. Carbon-bearing gases adsorb at the steel surface, dissociate, and diffuse inward to create a carbon concentration gradient. The metallurgical outcome relies on carbon diffusion into austenitized steel, followed by quenching to form a hardened martensitic surface layer. Industrial applications span automotive drivetrains, aerospace drive systems, transmission shafts, gears, bearings, and precision-machined components where surface durability and core toughness must coexist. Carburizing is a process whereby carbon is diffused into the surface of steel at high temperatures, where austenite is present, and the diffusion rate of carbon is reasonably high. Case carburizing steels are widely used in applications where high surface hardness is required in combination with good core toughness, high strength, and fatigue resistance. The depth of the hardened layer, known as the effective case depth (ECD), is controlled by temperature, carbon potential, and time in the furnace. Carburizing, quenching, and tempering increase surface hardness, wear resistance, fatigue strength, and tensile strength while producing the desired compressive residual stress at the surface. What Is Carburizing? Carburizing is a heat treatment process that diffuses carbon into the surface of steel at elevated temperatures to improve surface hardness and wear resistance. The process is commonly applied to low-carbon steels because the base metal needs a hard outer layer and a tough interior core. Carbon enters the steel surface during austenitizing, then moves inward through diffusion to create a controlled carbon concentration gradient. Quenching transforms the carbon-enriched surface into hardened martensite, which improves resistance against wear, pitting, and contact fatigue. Tempering follows quenching to reduce brittleness and stabilize the hardened case. Gears, shafts, bearings, pins, and drivetrain components use carburizing when surfaces face repeated friction, impact, or rolling contact. The core remains lower in carbon, which helps the part absorb shock without cracking under service loads. Carburized steel parts combine a hard case with a ductile core, making the process suitable for high-load mechanical components. Process control depends on carbon potential, temperature, holding time, quench medium, and required case depth. Why Does Carbon Increase Steel Hardness? Carbon increases steel hardness because higher carbon content promotes martensite formation during quenching. Austenitized steel dissolves carbon in the face-centered cubic structure before rapid cooling. Quenching traps carbon inside the body-centered tetragonal martensite structure, creating lattice strain that resists deformation. Higher carbon content increases the hardness of the martensitic case because the distorted crystal structure blocks dislocation movement. Wear resistance improves because the hardened surface resists abrasion, indentation, and rolling contact damage. Carburizing uses the effect by enriching the surface carbon level while keeping the core lower in carbon and tougher. Tempering follows quenching to reduce brittleness while keeping useful surface hardness for gears, shafts, bearings, and pins. Added carbon raises hardenability at the surface, so the treated case responds better to rapid cooling. The hardened case supports contact loads better because the carbon-enriched martensite resists plastic deformation. Excess carbon requires control because retained austenite or carbide networks reduce dimensional stability and toughness. Does Carburizing Harden the Entire Metal Component? Gas carburizing works by heating low-carbon steel in a furnace with a controlled carbon-rich atmosphere, then diffusing carbon into the steel surface. Methane, propane, natural gas, or endothermic carrier gas supplies carbon to the furnace atmosphere. The steel enters the austenitic temperature range, where the surface absorbs carbon-bearing gases. The gases dissociate at the surface, allowing carbon atoms to diffuse inward and form a carbon concentration gradient. Furnace carbon potential, temperature, and holding time control case depth and surface carbon level. Quenching follows carburizing to transform the carbon-enriched surface into hard martensite. Tempering reduces brittleness while keeping the wear-resistant case needed for gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts. Gas carburizing gives manufacturers consistent case hardening for a metal component that needs high surface durability and a tougher core. How Does the Carburizing Process Work? Vacuum carburizing differs from conventional carburizing because it uses a low-pressure furnace environment instead of a standard atmospheric furnace. The process introduces hydrocarbon gases (acetylene or propane) in controlled pulses at low pressure. Carbon diffuses into the steel surface under cleaner conditions because the furnace contains little oxygen and reduced gas contamination. The cleaner environment reduces oxidation, soot formation, and intergranular surface attack compared with conventional gas carburizing. Low-pressure control improves repeatability because temperature, pressure, gas flow, and boost diffusion cycles are closely regulated. Vacuum carburizing gives better case depth control for gears, shafts, bearings, fuel system parts, and aerospace components. The process needs precise quenching control because distortion risk still depends on part geometry, steel grade, and cooling severity. High-pressure gas quenching is commonly paired with vacuum carburizing to reduce oil contamination and improve part cleanliness. Complex parts benefit from vacuum carburizing when blind holes, narrow channels, or deep gear teeth require uniform carbon delivery. What Happens During Carbon Diffusion in Steel? During carbon diffusion in steel, carbon atoms migrate into the steel surface at elevated temperatures through atomic movement inside austenite. The steel surface absorbs carbon from a carbon-rich atmosphere, then carbon atoms move from the high-carbon surface into the lower-carbon interior. The movement creates a carbon concentration gradient, with the highest carbon level near the surface and a lower carbon level deeper in the part. Temperature increases atomic mobility, so carbon diffusion becomes faster inside the austenitic structure. Holding time controls how far carbon travels into the steel, which sets the final case depth. Quenching follows diffusion and transforms the carbon-enriched surface into hard martensite. The lower carbon core remains tougher, giving carburized parts a hard, wear-resistant case with a ductile interior. Longer diffusion time produces a deeper hardened case when temperature and carbon potential remain controlled. Excess surface carbon requires control because carbide networks or retained austenite reduce toughness and dimensional stability. Why Is Austenitizing Necessary Before Carburizing? Austenitizing is necessary before carburizing because steel must enter the austenitic structure to absorb and diffuse carbon effectively. Austenite has higher carbon solubility than ferrite, which allows carbon atoms to move into the surface during heat treatment. The elevated temperature increases atomic movement and helps create a controlled carbon concentration gradient. Carbon diffusion becomes limited when steel stays below the austenitizing range. Quenching after carburizing transforms the carbon-enriched austenite into hard martensite at the surface. The lower carbon core remains tougher, giving the part a hard case and ductile interior. Proper austenitizing improves case depth control by preparing the steel structure for uniform carbon movement. Insufficient austenitizing creates uneven carbon diffusion, which leads to inconsistent hardness after quenching. Controlled temperature and soak time help maintain the required balance from hardened surface to tough core. What Are the Main Types of Carburizing Processes? The main types of carburizing processes are listed below. Gas Carburizing: Gas carburizing is a surface chemistry process that improves the case depth hardness of a component by diffusing carbon into the surface layer to improve wear and fatigue resistance, using a gaseous carbon-rich atmosphere. The process runs at temperatures from 870°C to 930°C with hydrocarbons (methane or propane) as the carbon source, making it cost-effective for high-volume production. Pack Carburizing: Pack carburizing uses charcoal or carbon-containing powder sealed in a box, with the temperature range for carburizing at 870°C to 930°C. Carbon reacts with ambient air to form carbon dioxide and then carbon monoxide, which delivers carbon to the steel surface. Liquid Carburizing: Liquid carburizing is performed in salt baths (sodium cyanide), producing uniform surfaces and reducing oxide formation. The process is suited for small batches requiring consistent surface treatment across complex geometries. Vacuum Carburizing: The low-pressure carburizing (LPC) process takes place in a temperature range from 870°C to 1050°C with a pressure range from 5 mbar to 15 mbar, and during the complete process, the treated components are not exposed to any traces of oxygen. Plasma Carburizing: Plasma carburizing requires high equipment costs and is restricted to special carburizing treatments, such as those of parts having deep holes. The process uses ionized gas to deliver carbon to the steel surface under controlled electrical discharge conditions. How Does Gas Carburizing Work? Gas carburizing works by heating low-carbon steel in a furnace with a controlled carbon-rich atmosphere, then diffusing carbon into the steel surface. Methane, propane, natural gas, or endothermic carrier gas supplies carbon to the furnace atmosphere. The steel enters the austenitic temperature range, where the surface absorbs carbon-bearing gases. The gases dissociate at the surface, allowing carbon atoms to diffuse inward and form a carbon concentration gradient. Furnace carbon potential, temperature, and holding time control case depth and surface carbon level. Quenching follows carburizing to transform the carbon-enriched surface into hard martensite. Tempering reduces brittleness while keeping the wear-resistant case needed for gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts. Gas carburizing gives manufacturers consistent case hardening for steel components that need high surface durability and a tougher core. Process control keeps the carbon profile uniform across gear teeth, shaft shoulders, and bearing surfaces. Atmosphere monitoring prevents excess carbon pickup that leads to retained austenite, carbide networks, or dimensional instability. How Does Vacuum Carburizing Differ From Conventional Carburizing? Vacuum carburizing differs from conventional carburizing because it uses a low-pressure furnace environment instead of a standard atmospheric furnace. The process introduces hydrocarbon gases (acetylene or propane) in controlled pulses at low pressure. Carbon diffuses into the steel surface under cleaner conditions because the furnace contains little oxygen and reduced gas contamination. The cleaner environment reduces oxidation, soot formation, and intergranular surface attack compared with conventional gas carburizing. Low-pressure control improves repeatability because temperature, pressure, gas flow, and boost diffusion cycles are closely regulated. Vacuum carburizing gives better case depth control for gears, shafts, bearings, fuel system parts, and aerospace components. The process needs precise quenching control because distortion risk depends on part geometry, steel grade, and cooling severity. High-pressure gas quenching is commonly paired with vacuum carburizing to reduce oil contamination and improve part cleanliness. Complex geometries benefit from vacuum carburizing when blind holes, narrow channels, or deep gear teeth require controlled carbon delivery. Is Pack Carburizing One of the Oldest Carburizing Methods? Yes, pack carburizing is one of the oldest carburizing methods because it uses solid carbon materials to add carbon to steel surfaces. The process places low-carbon steel parts inside a sealed container filled with charcoal, coke, or carbon-rich powder. Heat causes carbon monoxide to form inside the pack, which reacts at the steel surface and supplies carbon for diffusion. The steel absorbs carbon at elevated temperatures, then develops a hardened case after quenching. Pack carburizing needs longer cycle times than gas or vacuum carburizing because carbon transfer and temperature control are slower. The method remains useful for simple parts, low-volume work, repair operations, and cases where advanced furnace atmosphere control is not required. What Materials Are Commonly Carburized? The materials that are commonly carburized are listed below. Low-Carbon Steels: Carburizing is performed on low-carbon steel at high temperatures where austenite is present, as the diffusion rate of carbon is reasonably high under those conditions. Steels with 0.10% to 0.25% carbon are the most frequently carburized, as they retain ductile cores after quenching. Alloy Steels: Alloy steels with manganese, chromium, and molybdenum additions respond well to carburizing because the alloying elements improve hardenability and support deeper martensitic transformation during quenching. Gear Steels: Carburizing is a widely used, effective technique to increase surface hardness of steel used in gears and achieve compressive residual stress, which contributes to long life and cost-effective production. Nickel-Chromium Steels: SAE 9310 steel, a high-nickel steel, is typically used in aircraft industry applications and other demanding applications, with nickel content improving core toughness and fatigue strength after carburizing and quenching. Chromium-Molybdenum Steels: Chromium-molybdenum steels (4118 or 8620) are carburized in aerospace and heavy equipment applications where high-strength cores combined with hard surfaces are required for drive components and shafts. Why Are Low-Carbon Steels Commonly Used for Carburizing? Low-carbon steels are commonly used for carburizing because they keep a ductile core while developing a hardened surface after carburizing and quenching. The low-carbon core absorbs impact and bending loads without cracking easily. Carbon enrichment increases surface carbon content, which allows martensite formation during quenching. The hardened case improves wear resistance, indentation resistance, and contact fatigue performance. The toughness difference from surface to core makes low-carbon steel suitable for gears, shafts, bearings, pins, and drivetrain parts. Medium-carbon or high-carbon steels already contain more carbon, so carburizing offers less benefit and higher distortion risk. Low-carbon steel gives manufacturers a practical balance of machinability, case hardness, and core toughness. The process allows parts to be machined before heat treatment, then hardened at the surface after final shaping. Alloying elements in low-carbon steels (nickel, chromium, and molybdenum) improve hardenability and support deeper case performance. Can High-Carbon Steels Be Carburized Effectively? No, high-carbon steels are not carburized effectively because they already contain enough carbon for hardening. Carburizing adds surface carbon, which increases the risk of excessive hardness, retained austenite, carbide networks, cracking, and distortion after quenching. High-carbon steel hardens through standard heat treatment without needing extra carbon diffusion at the surface. The process gives limited benefit when the core and surface already have high carbon content. Low-carbon steels remain the preferred choice because carburizing creates a hard case while preserving a tougher core. High-carbon steels suit through-hardening applications better than case hardening. Excess carbon at the surface makes quench response harder to control during final heat treatment. Tool steels and bearing steels usually need controlled hardening and tempering rather than added carbon diffusion. What Mechanical Properties Change During Carburizing? The mechanical properties that change during carburizing are listed below. Surface Hardness Increase: The results are increased surface hardness, wear resistance, fatigue strength, and localized case yield strength through carburizing and quenching plus tempering, as well as the desired compressive residual stress on the surface. Improved Wear Resistance: Gas carburizing improves the case depth hardness of a component by diffusing carbon into the surface layer to improve wear and fatigue resistance. The hardened martensitic case resists abrasion and rolling contact fatigue under repetitive loading. Improved Fatigue Strength: Carburizing is used to enhance fatigue resistance and toughness properties of dynamically loaded components. Compressive residual stresses in the case counteract tensile fatigue stresses during cyclic loading, extending the component's service life. Tough Core Retention: The core remains relatively soft and tough after quenching. Tempering is performed to increase the toughness and ductility of the quenched part. Higher Contact Stress Resistance: Carburizing is a widely used, effective technique to increase surface hardness of steel and achieve compressive residual stress, contributing to long life and cost-effective production. The hardened case supports high contact pressures in gear mesh and bearing race applications without surface yielding How Does Carburizing Improve Wear Resistance? Carburizing improves wear resistance by forming a hardened martensitic surface layer that resists abrasion, rolling contact fatigue, and surface deformation. Carbon diffusion raises the surface carbon level before quenching, which allows the outer case to transform into hard martensite. The hardened case resists scratching, pitting, scuffing, and indentation during sliding or rolling contact. The tougher low-carbon core supports impact loads without making the entire part is brittle. Gears, shafts, bearings, cams, and pins benefit from the hard case because the contact surface carries repeated friction and pressure. Tempering after quenching reduces brittleness while keeping the surface hardness needed for long service life. The hardened surface reduces material loss when parts move against mating components under load. The carbon-enriched case delays crack initiation on surfaces exposed to repeated contact stress. The core maintains toughness, so carburized parts resist sudden fracture better than through-hardened parts. Does Carburizing Improve Fatigue Life? Yes, carburizing improves fatigue life by creating a hard carbon-enriched case that resists surface crack initiation under repeated loading. The hardened martensitic surface reduces pitting, indentation, and rolling contact damage on gears, shafts, bearings, and cams. Compressive residual stress at the surface helps slow crack growth during cyclic service. The tougher core supports impact and bending loads without making the entire component brittle. Proper case depth, quench control, and tempering improve fatigue performance by balancing hardness with dimensional stability. Carburized parts gain longer service life when surface contact stress and repeated load cycles control failure risk. A uniform carbon gradient reduces weak transition zones from the hardened case to the core. Controlled tempering improves fatigue behavior by reducing quench stress while keeping surface hardness. You can design the perfect gear profile, but if you do not control the furnace atmosphere, you risk brittle carbide networks at the roots or unpredictable quench distortion that throws your tolerances out the window. True design for manufacturing means modeling the case gradient as part of the mechanical system, not just treating heat treatment as a post-processing afterthought." Audrius Zidonis PhD Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering What Equipment Is Used in Carburizing? The equipment that is used in the carburizing process is listed below. Controlled Atmosphere Furnaces: Sealed batch or continuous furnaces maintain precise hydrocarbon gas atmospheres at temperatures from 870°C to 930°C. Keeping all carburizing parameters, including temperature, carbon potential, and cycle time, under control is imperative to obtain a desired homogeneous carburizing case depth. Vacuum Furnaces: A vacuum furnace may be backfilled with a carburizing gas mixture after the load has been heated to the desired carburizing temperature, and vacuum furnaces are specifically suited for high-temperature carburizing. Quench Tanks: Oil quench tanks rapidly cool carburized parts from austenitizing temperature, freezing the high-carbon surface into martensite. High-pressure gas quenching is combined with vacuum carburizing, using quenching gas such as nitrogen or helium at 2 MPa, with quenching intensity controlled by gas pressure. Gas Delivery Systems: Precision flow control systems meter hydrocarbon feed gases (methane, propane, or acetylene) into the furnace chamber. The gas supply is modulated in accordance with the surface area of the part, helping to ensure that there are no uncarburized or over-carburized areas. Temperature Control Systems: Thermocouples and PID controllers maintain the furnace temperature within tight tolerances throughout the carburizing cycle. Temperature increases the diffusion rate, leading to a deeper case depth in less time than a case developed at a lower temperature. Carbon Potential Monitoring Equipment: Carbon control is critical to producing consistency in hardness, microstructure, and overall geometry. It is common practice to use in situ carbon probes to ensure proper control in achieving desired metallurgical results. How Do Furnaces Control Carbon Potential During Carburizing? Furnaces control carbon potential during carburizing by regulating the available carbon concentration at the steel surface. The furnace atmosphere supplies carbon through gases (methane, propane, carbon monoxide, or endothermic carrier gas). Oxygen probes, dew point sensors, and infrared gas analyzers monitor the atmosphere during the heat cycle. The control system adjusts gas flow to keep the carbon potential near the target surface carbon level. A high carbon potential increases carbon transfer, while excess carbon creates soot, retained austenite, or carbide networks. A low carbon potential reduces carbon absorption and produces shallow or uneven case depth. Temperature, soaking time, gas composition, and atmosphere circulation control the final carbon gradient. Accurate carbon potential control gives gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts a consistent hardened case after quenching. Stable atmosphere circulation helps maintain uniform carbon transfer across complex surfaces and deep gear teeth. Precise furnace control reduces case depth variation, surface defects, and post-quench hardness inconsistency. Does Quenching Occur After Carburizing? Yes, quenching occurs after carburizing because the carbon-enriched surface must transform into hard martensite. Carburizing raises the surface carbon level while the steel remains in the austenitic range. Rapid cooling locks carbon into the crystal structure and creates a hard, wear-resistant case. Oil, gas, or polymer quenching controls cooling speed depending on steel grade, part geometry, and distortion limits. The low-carbon core remains tougher than the hardened surface, which helps the part absorb impact and bending loads. Tempering usually follows quenching to reduce brittleness and stabilize hardness. Proper quench control reduces cracking, warping, and uneven hardness across the case. Cooling severity must match the part section size, alloy content, and required final hardness. Gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts rely on the hardened case produced by Quenching . What Are the Applications of Carburizing? The applications of carburizing are listed below. Automotive Gears: Automotive ring-and-pinion gears, truck transmission components, construction equipment drivetrains, and wind turbine gearbox stages all benefit from carburizing's combination of a deep hardened layer and tough core. Transmission Shafts: Transmission shafts carry torsional loads and require hard wear-resistant surfaces at spline interfaces and bearing journals while maintaining core ductility to resist shock loads during gear engagement. Bearings: Components (gears, camshafts, and bearings) commonly undergo carburizing to extend their service life under demanding conditions. Bearing races carburized to 58 to 62 HRC resist rolling contact fatigue across millions of load cycles in automotive and industrial service. Industrial Machine Components: Parts suitable for carburizing include bearings, bearing races, gears, and pinion shafts, which require a hard outer surface and a tough, fatigue-resistant core. Aerospace Drive Systems: Carburized parts offer superior fatigue performance and a more gradual hardness gradient than comparable induction-hardened parts. Heavy Equipment Wear Parts: Deep-case carburizing is essential for construction equipment with shock loads. Bucket teeth, track links, and drive sprockets on heavy machinery endure abrasive soil contact and impact, requiring deep carburized cases (up to 6.4 mm) for extended wear life. Why Is Carburizing Commonly Used for Gears and Bearings? Carburizing is commonly used for gears and bearings because the parts need hard, wear-resistant surfaces and impact-resistant cores. Gear teeth face sliding contact, rolling contact, and repeated load transfer during operation. Bearing surfaces face continuous pressure, friction, and fatigue stress from rolling elements or mating shafts. Carburizing creates a carbon-enriched martensitic case that resists pitting, scuffing, abrasion, and surface deformation. The lower carbon core stays tougher, which helps gears and bearings absorb shock loads without brittle fracture. Case depth control matters because shallow hardening wears too soon, while excessive case depth increases distortion risk. Quenching and tempering complete the process by setting surface hardness, reducing brittleness, and improving dimensional stability. Gearboxes, drivetrains, industrial machinery, and aerospace assemblies use carburized gears and bearings when long service life depends on strong surfaces and tough interiors. Proper carbon control helps gear teeth and bearing races maintain consistent hardness across contact zones. Uniform case hardening reduces early surface failure during repeated load cycles. Are Automotive Transmission Components Frequently Carburized? Yes, automotive transmission components are frequently carburized because gears, shafts, splines, and clutch hubs need hard wear-resistant surfaces with tough impact-resistant cores. Transmission gears face sliding contact, rolling contact, tooth bending stress, and repeated torque transfer during vehicle operation. Carburizing creates a hardened martensitic case that resists pitting, scuffing, abrasion, and surface deformation. The low-carbon core stays ductile enough to absorb shock loads from shifting, acceleration, and drivetrain vibration. Case depth control helps transmission parts maintain tooth strength without excessive distortion after quenching. Tempering reduces brittleness and improves dimensional stability after the hardening cycle. Automotive drivetrains use carburized components when long service life depends on surface durability and core toughness. How Does Carburizing Compare to Other Surface Hardening Processes? Carburizing compares to other surface hardening processes by adding carbon through diffusion at high austenitizing temperatures, while nitriding adds nitrogen at lower temperatures, induction hardening uses rapid localized heating, and carbonitriding adds carbon plus nitrogen. Carburizing produces a deep hardened case after quenching, making the process suitable for gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts. Nitriding forms a hard nitride layer without quenching, which reduces distortion and works well for wear-resistant precision parts. Induction hardening changes the surface microstructure through electromagnetic heating and quenching, but it does not add carbon or nitrogen to the steel. Carbonitriding uses a carbon and nitrogen-rich atmosphere at lower temperatures than carburizing, producing a thinner case with good wear resistance. Carburizing gives deeper case depth than nitriding and carbonitriding in many gear and shaft applications. Nitriding gives strong surface hardness with low distortion because the process temperature stays below the austenitizing range. Induction hardening works fastest for selective areas (gear teeth, bearing journals, and shaft shoulders). Carbonitriding suits small parts, fasteners, stampings, and low-carbon steel components needing a shallow hardened case. Process choice depends on required case depth, distortion limits, steel grade, surface hardness, production volume, and final part function. What Is the Difference Between Carburizing and Nitriding? The difference between carburizing and nitriding is that carburizing diffuses carbon into steel, while nitriding introduces nitrogen to form hard nitrides at the surface. Carburizing uses austenitizing temperatures and quenching to transform the carbon-enriched case into hard martensite. Nitriding uses lower temperatures and forms hard nitride compounds without a required quench. Carburizing produces deeper case depths for gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts that need high load capacity. Nitriding creates a thinner, very hard surface layer with lower distortion risk for precision parts. Carburizing suits low-carbon steels that need a tough core and wear-resistant surface. Nitriding suits alloy steels with nitride-forming elements (aluminum, chromium, molybdenum, and vanadium). Carburizing is chosen when heavy contact loads require deeper hardened support under the surface. Nitriding is chosen when dimensional stability and reduced distortion matter after final machining. Is Carburizing Deeper Than Induction Hardening? Yes, carburizing is deeper than induction hardening because carbon diffusion creates a hardened case below the steel surface. Carburizing case depth is controlled by temperature, carbon potential, and holding time. Induction hardening heats the surface rapidly through electromagnetic energy, then quenching hardens the heated layer. Induction hardening depth depends on frequency, power, heating time, and steel hardenability. Carburizing suits gears, shafts, and bearings that need deeper support under heavy contact loads. Induction hardening suits localized areas (shaft journals, gear teeth, and bearing seats) when fast surface hardening and reduced heat exposure matter. Case depth selection depends on load, wear pattern, geometry, distortion limits, and final performance requirements. Carburized cases give gradual hardness support below the surface, which helps resist subsurface fatigue under repeated rolling contact. Induction-hardened layers offer faster processing, but hardened depth remains more limited by heating pattern and frequency control. What Are the Limitations of Carburizing? The limitations of Carburizing are distortion risk, long processing times, dimensional changes, and limited suitability for certain alloys. High carburizing temperatures and quenching create thermal gradients, phase changes, and residual stress that shift precision features from final dimensions. Gear teeth, bearing races, shafts, and splines need post-heat treatment inspection because carburizing changes part size and shape. Carburizing takes longer than induction hardening or carbonitriding because carbon must diffuse into the steel surface over time. Process time increases when deeper case depth is required, depending on temperature and holding time. High-carbon steels and tool steels are poor candidates because excess surface carbon raises the risk of carbide networks, retained austenite, cracking, and unstable hardness. Low-carbon alloy steels remain better choices when parts need a hard case and tough core. Post-carburizing grinding or finishing becomes necessary when tight tolerances or surface finish requirements matter. Process control must account for furnace atmosphere, quench medium, part geometry, and alloy response before production approval. Why Can Carburizing Cause Distortion in Steel Parts? Carburizing distorts steel parts because high-temperature exposure and quenching create thermal stresses, phase changes, and dimensional movement. The part expands during heating, then contracts unevenly during cooling. Quenching cools thin sections faster than thick sections, which creates uneven stress across the part. Austenite transforms into martensite during rapid cooling, and the volume change shifts the final dimensions. Gears, shafts, splines, and bearing races are sensitive because precise surfaces move under heat treatment stress. Sharp corners, uneven wall thickness, and complex shapes increase distortion risk during quenching. Controlled heating, uniform fixturing, proper quench selection, and post-treatment grinding reduce dimensional variation after carburizing. Residual stresses remain after quenching when different sections cool and transform at different rates. Distortion control requires part-specific fixtures, balanced geometry, controlled quench agitation, and inspection after heat treatment. Can Excessive Carburizing Increase Brittleness? Yes, excessive carburizing increases brittleness. Case depths that are too deep lead to through carburizing of the tooth, resulting in loss of ductility and reduced fatigue life. Quench embrittlement negatively affects the relationship between hardness to ultimate tensile strength, especially at high hardness and elevated steel carbon levels. The plastic portion of the stress-strain curve is reduced or eliminated, causing the steel to fail in a brittle manner. Tempering at 300°F to 400°F reduces brittleness while preserving hardness, strength, compressive residual stress, and fatigue life. Controlling carbon potential and case depth within specified limits is mandatory to prevent brittleness while retaining the fatigue and wear performance gains that carburizing delivers. Excess carbon creates carbide networks that interrupt the hardened case structure and reduce impact resistance. Metallurgical inspection verifies surface carbon level, effective case depth, and hardness profile before the part enters service. sections.text: What Is Carburizing? Carburizing is a heat treatment process that diffuses carbon into the surface of steel at elevated temperatures to improve surface hardness and wear resistance. The process is commonly applied to low-carbon steels because the base metal needs a hard outer layer and a tough interior core. Carbon enters the steel surface during austenitizing, then moves inward through diffusion to create a controlled carbon concentration gradient. Quenching transforms the carbon-enriched surface into hardened martensite, which improves resistance against wear, pitting, and contact fatigue. Tempering follows quenching to reduce brittleness and stabilize the hardened case. Gears, shafts, bearings, pins, and drivetrain components use carburizing when surfaces face repeated friction, impact, or rolling contact. The core remains lower in carbon, which helps the part absorb shock without cracking under service loads. Carburized steel parts combine a hard case with a ductile core, making the process suitable for high-load mechanical components. Process control depends on carbon potential, temperature, holding time, quench medium, and required case depth.

sections.heading: Why Does Carbon Increase Steel Hardness?
sections.text: Why Does Carbon Increase Steel Hardness? Carbon increases steel hardness because higher carbon content promotes martensite formation during quenching. Austenitized steel dissolves carbon in the face-centered cubic structure before rapid cooling. Quenching traps carbon inside the body-centered tetragonal martensite structure, creating lattice strain that resists deformation. Higher carbon content increases the hardness of the martensitic case because the distorted crystal structure blocks dislocation movement. Wear resistance improves because the hardened surface resists abrasion, indentation, and rolling contact damage. Carburizing uses the effect by enriching the surface carbon level while keeping the core lower in carbon and tougher. Tempering follows quenching to reduce brittleness while keeping useful surface hardness for gears, shafts, bearings, and pins. Added carbon raises hardenability at the surface, so the treated case responds better to rapid cooling. The hardened case supports contact loads better because the carbon-enriched martensite resists plastic deformation. sections.heading: How Does the Carburizing Process Work?
sections.text: How Does the Carburizing Process Work? Vacuum carburizing differs from conventional carburizing because it uses a low-pressure furnace environment instead of a standard atmospheric furnace. The process introduces hydrocarbon gases (acetylene or propane) in controlled pulses at low pressure. Carbon diffuses into the steel surface under cleaner conditions because the furnace contains little oxygen and reduced gas contamination. The cleaner environment reduces oxidation, soot formation, and intergranular surface attack compared with conventional gas carburizing. Low-pressure control improves repeatability because temperature, pressure, gas flow, and boost diffusion cycles are closely regulated. Vacuum carburizing gives better case depth control for gears, shafts, bearings, fuel system parts, and aerospace components. The process needs precise quenching control because distortion risk still depends on part geometry, steel grade, and cooling severity. High-pressure gas quenching is commonly paired with vacuum carburizing to reduce oil contamination and improve part cleanliness. sections.heading: What Happens During Carbon Diffusion in Steel?
sections.text: What Happens During Carbon Diffusion in Steel? During carbon diffusion in steel, carbon atoms migrate into the steel surface at elevated temperatures through atomic movement inside austenite. The steel surface absorbs carbon from a carbon-rich atmosphere, then carbon atoms move from the high-carbon surface into the lower-carbon interior. The movement creates a carbon concentration gradient, with the highest carbon level near the surface and a lower carbon level deeper in the part. Temperature increases atomic mobility, so carbon diffusion becomes faster inside the austenitic structure. Holding time controls how far carbon travels into the steel, which sets the final case depth. Quenching follows diffusion and transforms the carbon-enriched surface into hard martensite. The lower carbon core remains tougher, giving carburized parts a hard, wear-resistant case with a ductile interior. Longer diffusion time produces a deeper hardened case when temperature and carbon potential remain controlled. sections.heading: What Are the Main Types of Carburizing Processes?
sections.text: What Are the Main Types of Carburizing Processes? The main types of carburizing processes are listed below. Gas Carburizing: Gas carburizing is a surface chemistry process that improves the case depth hardness of a component by diffusing carbon into the surface layer to improve wear and fatigue resistance, using a gaseous carbon-rich atmosphere. The process runs at temperatures from 870°C to 930°C with hydrocarbons (methane or propane) as the carbon source, making it cost-effective for high-volume production. Pack Carburizing: Pack carburizing uses charcoal or carbon-containing powder sealed in a box, with the temperature range for carburizing at 870°C to 930°C. Carbon reacts with ambient air to form carbon dioxide and then carbon monoxide, which delivers carbon to the steel surface. Liquid Carburizing: Liquid carburizing is performed in salt baths (sodium cyanide), producing uniform surfaces and reducing oxide formation. The process is suited for small batches requiring consistent surface treatment across complex geometries. Vacuum Carburizing: The low-pressure carburizing (LPC) process takes place in a temperature range from 870°C to 1050°C with a pressure range from 5 mbar to 1...

sections.heading: How Does Gas Carburizing Work?
sections.text: How Does Gas Carburizing Work? Gas carburizing works by heating low-carbon steel in a furnace with a controlled carbon-rich atmosphere, then diffusing carbon into the steel surface. Methane, propane, natural gas, or endothermic carrier gas supplies carbon to the furnace atmosphere. The steel enters the austenitic temperature range, where the surface absorbs carbon-bearing gases. The gases dissociate at the surface, allowing carbon atoms to diffuse inward and form a carbon concentration gradient. Furnace carbon potential, temperature, and holding time control case depth and surface carbon level. Quenching follows carburizing to transform the carbon-enriched surface into hard martensite. Tempering reduces brittleness while keeping the wear-resistant case needed for gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts. Gas carburizing gives manufacturers consistent case hardening for steel components that need high surface durability and a tougher core. Process control keeps the carbon profile uniform across gear teeth, shaft shoulders, and bearing surfaces. Atmosphere monitoring prevents excess carbon pickup that leads to retained austenite, carbide networks, or dimensional instability.

sections.heading: What Materials Are Commonly Carburized?
sections.text: What Materials Are Commonly Carburized? The materials that are commonly carburized are listed below. Low-Carbon Steels: Carburizing is performed on low-carbon steel at high temperatures where austenite is present, as the diffusion rate of carbon is reasonably high under those conditions. Steels with 0.10% to 0.25% carbon are the most frequently carburized, as they retain ductile cores after quenching. Alloy Steels: Alloy steels with manganese, chromium, and molybdenum additions respond well to carburizing because the alloying elements improve hardenability and support deeper martensitic transformation during quenching. Gear Steels: Carburizing is a widely used, effective technique to increase surface hardness of steel used in gears and achieve compressive residual stress, which contributes to long life and cost-effective production. Nickel-Chromium Steels: SAE 9310 steel, a high-nickel steel, is typically used in aircraft industry applications and other demanding applications, with nickel content improving core toughness and fatigue strength after carburizing and quenching. Chromium-Molybdenum Steels: Chromium-molybdenum steels (4118 or 8620) are carburized in aerospace and heavy...

sections.heading: Why Are Low-Carbon Steels Commonly Used for Carburizing?
sections.text: Why Are Low-Carbon Steels Commonly Used for Carburizing? Low-carbon steels are commonly used for carburizing because they keep a ductile core while developing a hardened surface after carburizing and quenching. The low-carbon core absorbs impact and bending loads without cracking easily. Carbon enrichment increases surface carbon content, which allows martensite formation during quenching. The hardened case improves wear resistance, indentation resistance, and contact fatigue performance. The toughness difference from surface to core makes low-carbon steel suitable for gears, shafts, bearings, pins, and drivetrain parts. Medium-carbon or high-carbon steels already contain more carbon, so carburizing offers less benefit and higher distortion risk. Low-carbon steel gives manufacturers a practical balance of machinability, case hardness, and core toughness. The process allows parts to be machined before heat treatment, then hardened at the surface after final shaping. Alloying elements in low-carbon steels (nickel, chromium, and molybdenum) improve hardenability and support deeper case performance. Can High-Carbon Steels Be Carburized Effectively? No, high-carbon steels are not carbu...

sections.heading: What Mechanical Properties Change During Carburizing?
sections.text: What Mechanical Properties Change During Carburizing? The mechanical properties that change during carburizing are listed below. Surface Hardness Increase: The results are increased surface hardness, wear resistance, fatigue strength, and localized case yield strength through carburizing and quenching plus tempering, as well as the desired compressive residual stress on the surface. Improved Wear Resistance: Gas carburizing improves the case depth hardness of a component by diffusing carbon into the surface layer to improve wear and fatigue resistance. The hardened martensitic case resists abrasion and rolling contact fatigue under repetitive loading. Improved Fatigue Strength: Carburizing is used to enhance fatigue resistance and toughness properties of dynamically loaded components. Compressive residual stresses in the case counteract tensile fatigue stresses during cyclic loading, extending the component's service life. Tough Core Retention: The core remains relatively soft and tough after quenching. Tempering is performed to increase the toughness and ductility of the quenched part. Higher Contact Stress Resistance: Carburizing is a widely used, effective technique to increase...

sections.heading: How Does Carburizing Improve Wear Resistance?
sections.text: How Does Carburizing Improve Wear Resistance? Carburizing improves wear resistance by forming a hardened martensitic surface layer that resists abrasion, rolling contact fatigue, and surface deformation. Carbon diffusion raises the surface carbon level before quenching, which allows the outer case to transform into hard martensite. The hardened case resists scratching, pitting, scuffing, and indentation during sliding or rolling contact. The tougher low-carbon core supports impact loads without making the entire part is brittle. Gears, shafts, bearings, cams, and pins benefit from the hard case because the contact surface carries repeated friction and pressure. Tempering after quenching reduces brittleness while keeping the surface hardness needed for long service life. The hardened surface reduces material loss when parts move against mating components under load. The carbon-enriched case delays crack initiation on surfaces exposed to repeated contact stress. The core maintains toughness, so carburized parts resist sudden fracture better than through-hardened parts. Does Carburizing Improve Fatigue Life? Yes, carburizing improves fatigue life by creating a hard carbon-enriched ca...

sections.heading: What Equipment Is Used in Carburizing?
sections.text: What Equipment Is Used in Carburizing? The equipment that is used in the carburizing process is listed below. Controlled Atmosphere Furnaces: Sealed batch or continuous furnaces maintain precise hydrocarbon gas atmospheres at temperatures from 870°C to 930°C. Keeping all carburizing parameters, including temperature, carbon potential, and cycle time, under control is imperative to obtain a desired homogeneous carburizing case depth. Vacuum Furnaces: A vacuum furnace may be backfilled with a carburizing gas mixture after the load has been heated to the desired carburizing temperature, and vacuum furnaces are specifically suited for high-temperature carburizing. Quench Tanks: Oil quench tanks rapidly cool carburized parts from austenitizing temperature, freezing the high-carbon surface into martensite. High-pressure gas quenching is combined with vacuum carburizing, using quenching gas such as nitrogen or helium at 2 MPa, with quenching intensity controlled by gas pressure. Gas Delivery Systems: Precision flow control systems meter hydrocarbon feed gases (methane, propane, or acetylene) into the furnace chamber. The gas supply is modulated in accordance with the surface area of the...

sections.heading: How Do Furnaces Control Carbon Potential During Carburizing?
sections.text: How Do Furnaces Control Carbon Potential During Carburizing? Furnaces control carbon potential during carburizing by regulating the available carbon concentration at the steel surface. The furnace atmosphere supplies carbon through gases (methane, propane, carbon monoxide, or endothermic carrier gas). Oxygen probes, dew point sensors, and infrared gas analyzers monitor the atmosphere during the heat cycle. The control system adjusts gas flow to keep the carbon potential near the target surface carbon level. A high carbon potential increases carbon transfer, while excess carbon creates soot, retained austenite, or carbide networks. A low carbon potential reduces carbon absorption and produces shallow or uneven case depth. Temperature, soaking time, gas composition, and atmosphere circulation control the final carbon gradient. Accurate carbon potential control gives gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts a consistent hardened case after quenching. Stable atmosphere circulation helps maintain uniform carbon transfer across complex surfaces and deep gear teeth. sections.heading: What Are the Applications of Carburizing?
sections.text: What Are the Applications of Carburizing? The applications of carburizing are listed below. Automotive Gears: Automotive ring-and-pinion gears, truck transmission components, construction equipment drivetrains, and wind turbine gearbox stages all benefit from carburizing's combination of a deep hardened layer and tough core. Transmission Shafts: Transmission shafts carry torsional loads and require hard wear-resistant surfaces at spline interfaces and bearing journals while maintaining core ductility to resist shock loads during gear engagement. Bearings: Components (gears, camshafts, and bearings) commonly undergo carburizing to extend their service life under demanding conditions. Bearing races carburized to 58 to 62 HRC resist rolling contact fatigue across millions of load cycles in automotive and industrial service. Industrial Machine Components: Parts suitable for carburizing include bearings, bearing races, gears, and pinion shafts, which require a hard outer surface and a tough, fatigue-resistant core. Aerospace Drive Systems: Carburized parts offer superior fatigue performance and a more gradual hardness gradient than comparable induction-hardened parts. Heavy Equipment W...

sections.heading: Why Is Carburizing Commonly Used for Gears and Bearings?
sections.text: Why Is Carburizing Commonly Used for Gears and Bearings? Carburizing is commonly used for gears and bearings because the parts need hard, wear-resistant surfaces and impact-resistant cores. Gear teeth face sliding contact, rolling contact, and repeated load transfer during operation. Bearing surfaces face continuous pressure, friction, and fatigue stress from rolling elements or mating shafts. Carburizing creates a carbon-enriched martensitic case that resists pitting, scuffing, abrasion, and surface deformation. The lower carbon core stays tougher, which helps gears and bearings absorb shock loads without brittle fracture. Case depth control matters because shallow hardening wears too soon, while excessive case depth increases distortion risk. Quenching and tempering complete the process by setting surface hardness, reducing brittleness, and improving dimensional stability. Gearboxes, drivetrains, industrial machinery, and aerospace assemblies use carburized gears and bearings when long service life depends on strong surfaces and tough interiors. Proper carbon control helps gear teeth and bearing races maintain consistent hardness across contact zones. Uniform case hardening redu...

sections.heading: How Does Carburizing Compare to Other Surface Hardening Processes?
sections.text: How Does Carburizing Compare to Other Surface Hardening Processes? Carburizing compares to other surface hardening processes by adding carbon through diffusion at high austenitizing temperatures, while nitriding adds nitrogen at lower temperatures, induction hardening uses rapid localized heating, and carbonitriding adds carbon plus nitrogen. Carburizing produces a deep hardened case after quenching, making the process suitable for gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts. Nitriding forms a hard nitride layer without quenching, which reduces distortion and works well for wear-resistant precision parts. Induction hardening changes the surface microstructure through electromagnetic heating and quenching, but it does not add carbon or nitrogen to the steel. Carbonitriding uses a carbon and nitrogen-rich atmosphere at lower temperatures than carburizing, producing a thinner case with good wear resistance. Carburizing gives deeper case depth than nitriding and carbonitriding in many gear and shaft applications. Nitriding gives strong surface hardness with low distortion because the process temperature stays below the austenitizing range. Induction hardening works fastest for selec...

sections.heading: What Is the Difference Between Carburizing and Nitriding?
sections.text: What Is the Difference Between Carburizing and Nitriding? The difference between carburizing and nitriding is that carburizing diffuses carbon into steel, while nitriding introduces nitrogen to form hard nitrides at the surface. Carburizing uses austenitizing temperatures and quenching to transform the carbon-enriched case into hard martensite. Nitriding uses lower temperatures and forms hard nitride compounds without a required quench. Carburizing produces deeper case depths for gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts that need high load capacity. Nitriding creates a thinner, very hard surface layer with lower distortion risk for precision parts. Carburizing suits low-carbon steels that need a tough core and wear-resistant surface. Nitriding suits alloy steels with nitride-forming elements (aluminum, chromium, molybdenum, and vanadium). Carburizing is chosen when heavy contact loads require deeper hardened support under the surface. Nitriding is chosen when dimensional stability and reduced distortion matter after final machining. sections.heading: What Are the Limitations of Carburizing?
sections.text: What Are the Limitations of Carburizing? The limitations of Carburizing are distortion risk, long processing times, dimensional changes, and limited suitability for certain alloys. High carburizing temperatures and quenching create thermal gradients, phase changes, and residual stress that shift precision features from final dimensions. Gear teeth, bearing races, shafts, and splines need post-heat treatment inspection because carburizing changes part size and shape. Carburizing takes longer than induction hardening or carbonitriding because carbon must diffuse into the steel surface over time. Process time increases when deeper case depth is required, depending on temperature and holding time. High-carbon steels and tool steels are poor candidates because excess surface carbon raises the risk of carbide networks, retained austenite, cracking, and unstable hardness. Low-carbon alloy steels remain better choices when parts need a hard case and tough core. Post-carburizing grinding or finishing becomes necessary when tight tolerances or surface finish requirements matter. sections.heading: Why Can Carburizing Cause Distortion in Steel Parts?
sections.text: Why Can Carburizing Cause Distortion in Steel Parts? Carburizing distorts steel parts because high-temperature exposure and quenching create thermal stresses, phase changes, and dimensional movement. The part expands during heating, then contracts unevenly during cooling. Quenching cools thin sections faster than thick sections, which creates uneven stress across the part. Austenite transforms into martensite during rapid cooling, and the volume change shifts the final dimensions. Gears, shafts, splines, and bearing races are sensitive because precise surfaces move under heat treatment stress. Sharp corners, uneven wall thickness, and complex shapes increase distortion risk during quenching. Controlled heating, uniform fixturing, proper quench selection, and post-treatment grinding reduce dimensional variation after carburizing. Residual stresses remain after quenching when different sections cool and transform at different rates.
